'''''Rosa setigera''''', commonly known as the '''climbing rose''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=ROSE2|taxon=Rosa setigera|accessdate=14 July 2019}}</ref> '''prairie rose''',<ref name=natureserve/> and '''climbing wild rose''',<ref name="IL">{{cite web |title=Climbing Wild Rose (Rosa setigera) |url=https://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/savanna/plants/wc_rose.htm |website=www.illinoiswildflowers.info}}</ref> is a species of [[shrub]] or [[vine]] in the [[Rosaceae]] (rose) family native to central and eastern North America.

==Description==
''R. setigera'' has trailing or climbing slender stems that grow up to {{convert |15|ft|m|0| order=flip}} long.<ref>{{cite web |title=Rosa setigera - Plant Finder |url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=g860 |website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}}</ref> The plant grows either as a vine or forms a sprawling thicket.<ref name=MO>{{cite book |last1=Denison |first1=Edgar |title=Missouri Wildflowers |date=2017 |publisher=Conservation Commission of the State of Missouri |isbn=978-1-887247-59-7 |pages=62 |edition=Sixth}}</ref> In open areas, the stems will arch downward after reaching a height of about {{convert |3|ft|m|0| order=flip}}, and where they touch the ground they will root. In areas with vegetation or other structures, the stems will tend to climb.<ref name="IL"/> The stems are green or brown with a reddish tint and have curved [[thorns, spines, and prickles|prickles]].<ref name=s>{{cite book |last1=Ogle|last2=Witsell|last3=Gentry |first1=Jennifer|first2=Theo|first3=Johnnie |title=Trees Shrubs and Woody Vines of Arkansas |date=2020|publisher=The Ozark Society Foundation |isbn=9780912456003 |pages=382}}</ref>

The leaves are alternate and compound, with 3 to 5 leaflets on each leaf. Each leaf is {{convert |8-12|cm|in|1|}} long, with leaflets that are {{convert |3-5|cm|in|1}} long and {{convert |1.5-4|cm|in|1|}} wide. Leaflets are [[Glossary_of_botanical_terms#ovate|ovate]], with [[serrate]] or doubly serrate margins.<ref name=s/>

The fragrant flowers, blooming May to July, are usually pink, occasionally white, and appear either singly or in groups, or [[panicles]] on stalks. Each flower, measuring about {{convert |8|cm|in|0}} wide, has large petals and many [[stamens]].<ref name=MO/> The fruit appears later in the summer as bright red rose hips.<ref name=s/>

Setigera's range overlaps with several other Rosa species, as well as some invasives. It can be differentiated from Rosa Multiflora by its tendency to have pink flowers. Multiflora only produces white flowers. Their rosehips are fairly comparable. Dog Rose (Rosa Canina) can also have small pink flowers, but their rosehips are large and more cylindrical. Rosa Setigera can also be differentiated from another native, Rose Carolina, by the fact that Carolina tends to grow lower to the ground and has larger flowers and rosehips.

==Distribution and habitat==
''R. setigera'' is native in the United States from Texas and Nebraska in the west, Wisconsin in the north, New Hampshire in the east, and Florida in the south. It is also native to Ontario and is listed as a species of special concern because of loss of habitat.<ref name="natureserve"/> The plant can be found in areas with average to moist, well-drained soils, including forests and woodlands, roadsides, bluffs, streambanks, old fields, and pastures.<ref name=s/>

==Ecology==
The flowers bloom in the spring to summer, with rose hips following later in the summer. Bees pollinate the flowers, and various other insects feed on the plant. Birds and mammals eat the hips.<ref name=IL/> ''R. setigera'' is the larval host for several species of moths, including ''[[Paleacrita vernata]]'' (spring cankerworm), ''[[Stigmella rosaefoliella]]'', and ''[[Coptotriche roseticola]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |title=HOSTS - The Hostplants and Caterpillars Database at the Natural History Museum |url=https://www.nhm.ac.uk/our-science/data/hostplants/search/list.dsml?searchPageURL=index.dsml&Familyqtype=starts+with&Family=&PFamilyqtype=starts+with&PFamily=&Genusqtype=starts+with&Genus=&PGenusqtype=starts+with&PGenus=rosa&Speciesqtype=starts+with&Species=&PSpeciesqtype=starts+with&PSpecies=setigera&Country=&sort=Family |website=www.nhm.ac.uk| date=2023 | doi=10.5519/havt50xw | last1=Robinson | first1=Gaden S. | last2=Ackery | first2=Phillip R. | last3=Kitching | first3=Ian | last4=Beccaloni | first4=George W. | last5=Hernández | first5=Luis M. }}</ref>
